question: What is the time difference between the actual passing of the Sun over the horizon and our being able to see the image of it on earth?
solution:
The correct answer is __**2 min**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The time difference between the actual passing of the Sun over the horizon and our being able to see the image of it on Earth is approximately **2 minutes**.
 
• This phenomenon occurs due to the **refraction of light** in Earth's atmosphere.
 
• As light from the Sun enters Earth's atmosphere, it is bent or refracted, causing the Sun to appear slightly higher in the sky than it actually is.
 
• This effect allows us to see the Sun for a few minutes before it has actually risen and a few minutes after it has actually set.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Refraction:**

 
 
• Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another with different densities.
 
• In the context of the Sun's image, light travels from the vacuum of space into Earth's atmosphere, which has a higher density.
 
• This bending causes the light to change direction, making the Sun appear to be at a different position than where it actually is.
 
 
 
• **Atmospheric Refraction:**
 
 
• Atmospheric refraction is the effect of Earth's atmosphere on the apparent position of celestial objects.
 
• It is most noticeable during sunrise and sunset, when the path of sunlight through the atmosphere is longest.
 
• This phenomenon also causes the apparent flattening of the Sun's disk near the horizon.
 
 
 
• **Twilight:**
 
 
• Twilight is the time period during which the Sun is below the horizon but its light is scattered in the upper atmosphere.
 
• There are three types of twilight: civil, nautical, and astronomical, each defined by the position of the Sun relative to the horizon.
 
• Refraction plays a key role in extending the duration of twilight by allowing the Sun's light to reach the observer before it has actually risen and after it has set.
